cells.tense: Your hands are on the work and your attention is on the person in front of you at the same time.
cells.ask: Name one thing you'll keep doing for a specific person, and say it to them this week — small, decided, no new effort.
cells.core:
You can stay with one person or one piece of work for a long time and still be reachable while you do it. Most people lose one when they hold the other — they go distant, or they scatter. You've found the narrow line where dedication makes you more present instead of less. The person in front of you gets the steady version, not the distracted one.

What that looks like when it's going well: you notice what someone is carrying without being told, you keep showing up past the point where it stops being interesting, and neither of those runs you down. The work has taught you how to feel with people, which is a strange kind of gift but it's yours. Keep both fed. The practice and the person grow on the same attention, and neither one needs rushing to hold.
cells.sheetLine: Steady dedication and open connection, both real at once.
cells.verb: kept at the same fire through every deepening pass
cells.place: in the room where one person's weather becomes yours to feel

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a future version of this relationship that hasn't arrived and can't be written in.
cells.ask: Share something small with one other person that has nothing to do with progress — say it out loud, then stop.
cells.core:
You're working ahead of where the relationship actually is. Reading the next five moves, preparing for what you'll need to hold, bracing for the weight before anyone hands it to you. The dedicated practice that usually grounds you has turned into a running forecast, and the forecast is eating the present moment.

What your persistence is for is deeper mastery, not wider control. Pushing harder in the same direction won't get you there. Take the next thing you're refining and set it in front of somebody as a shared moment, not a progress report. Let it land as something you enjoy together, without it having to prove anything about where it's heading. Joy shared is the correction here, and it asks you to loosen your grip on the outcome.
cells.sheetLine: You're rehearsing a future no one gave you yet.

cells.tense: You stopped showing the person what you were actually building, and that door is behind you now.
cells.ask: Put one thing you've made or kept in front of one person, exactly as it is, and let it speak without you explaining it.
cells.core:
The practice continued, quietly. The sharing of it stopped. So now the connection feels thin — you keep steady, you do the work, but the person in front of you doesn't see the person doing it. You're present in the room and absent from it at the same time, and that gap has been there long enough to feel like your own shape.

Feeling more is not the assignment. Showing one plain piece of what you've carried is. Not vulnerable, not a confession: just the thing itself, set down where someone can see it. Your competence is real. Let it come forward as something the relationship can lean on, and whatever you've been holding under the surface will have somewhere to go.

cells.tense: You are already the one setting the shape of the room, and you've been describing it as the situation making you do it.
cells.ask: Speak one sentence starting with 'I keep this going' about something you've been calling the work or what the moment needed.
cells.core:
You've been showing up for a long time. People come to you before decisions settle, and they take how you hold yourself as the shape of the room. That's real, and it's yours. The way you describe it, though, sounds like the situation is moving you — 'this is just what the moment needed,' as if you weren't the one at the wheel.

Underneath the persistence is a simpler thing: you move from what you genuinely feel. When you let that be your reason, the momentum gets quieter and more certain. One honest sentence about what you keep choosing will do more than another month of carrying it while calling it circumstance. Saying it in your own voice puts the pen back in your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You're already the one steering. Say it plainly once.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person attributes an ongoing practice to circumstance rather than to their own authorship; the record says authorship is misattributed, not that the practice is called external. Reader's likely objection: 'This is my job — I didn't choose the caring, it's what's in front of me.' The ask survives being wrong: naming one act of persistence as one's own still returns authorship even if the practice is smaller or more chosen than I read. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person: 'You've built something here that most people couldn't.' That flatters and tells them nothing they can pick up.
